prompt: Why didn't Harvard have calculus classes when it first opened?
answer:
Harvard was founded in 1636, while calculus was not developed until the late 1600s—mainly through the work of Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in the 1660s–1680s.

Harvard’s early curriculum focused on classical education: Latin and Greek, theology, rhetoric, philosophy, logic, arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy. Its main purpose was to educate ministers and civic leaders, not to teach advanced mathematics. So Harvard had no calculus classes initially both because calculus did not yet exist as a formal subject and because it was outside the college’s original educational goals.
